header.name: Xavier Lacroix
header.role: Computer science student at INSA Lyon
header.bio: I've been a computer science student at INSA Lyon since September 2026. Before that: three years of the BUT Informatique at IUT Lyon 1 (AGED track), including a one-year apprenticeship as a Data Analyst at Lysarc, working on a national clinical registry. Alongside that, I build a lot of personal projects — websites, a homelab, AI agents. What I'm into: data, systems, and turning an idea into something that actually runs. My aim: Data Engineer and AI Engineer roles.

lysarc.title: The company: Lysarc
body: Lysarc (The Lymphoma Academic Research Organisation) is a French non-profit, the academic research arm of the Lysa network — dedicated to lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and Waldenström's disease. It is the world's largest academic research structure focused on lymphomas, based at CHU Lyon Sud. It launches four to six new clinical trials a year alongside around fifty ongoing studies.

During my apprenticeship the organisation went through a leadership change and a structural reorganisation: a new strategic roadmap, the creation of an innovation hub and of a department dedicated to clinical data engineering and programming. That reorganisation is what made my missions shift over the year.

I was the only Data Analyst in the organisation: no peer in the role, no established methodology to inherit, no technical referent on my own toolchain. That autonomy was a driver — it forced me to choose, document and justify every decision, which is why documentation and training come attached to every one of my deliverables.

environnement.title: Technical environment
environnement.intro: The registry's data is not a volume problem: it fits on a workstation. The work is organised around two refresh chains, at two cadences and two levels of reliability.
items: A weekly raw export from the clinical data-capture tool (Ennov), underived — it feeds the Power BI dashboards and operational steering.
A chain of SAS derivations and exclusions, on a roughly six-month cadence — it produces the analysis datasets for the official statistical reports.

Windows workstation, SAS and Power BI Desktop for analysis, Power BI Cloud for distribution, Visual Studio Code and Git for Python development, and internal infrastructure for running language models locally.

A significant part of my documentation and training work was to make the distinction between these two chains explicit, so that operational figures are never confused with official statistical figures.
